Numbered badges show the search running down one branch, A, B, D, F, E, before backing up to reach C last; the accent edges form a single long path. The result card lists the order A, B, D, F, E, C." width="100%"} DFS follows one branch as deep as it can go before backtracking to the most recent node that still has unvisited neighbors. Neighbors are tried in the order their edges were added, so on a tree the traversal produces a pre-order listing. On a directed graph only outgoing edges are followed, so the traversal covers exactly the nodes reachable from `source=`; nodes that cannot be reached are never visited. Common reasons to run a DFS: - exploring a hierarchy branch by branch (pre-order listing of a tree) - listing everything reachable from a node - producing a visit order to color or animate, as a contrast to the layered order of `bfs()` By default the visit order is stored on the graph as a node attribute and the graph is returned for chaining. Set `return_list=True` to get the visit order directly instead. Either way, the traversal is also recorded in the graph's step log (`steps`), so it can be replayed node by node with `play()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to start the traversal from, given as an integer node ID or a string label. It is always the first node visited (position `0`). [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute that receives each node's position in the traversal. If `None` (default), the attribute is called `dfs_order`. Positions are 0-indexed, so the start node gets `0`, the next node visited gets `1`, and so on. Nodes the traversal does not reach get no value. An existing attribute with the same name is overwritten. Ignored when `return_list=True`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `False` (default), store the positions as a node attribute (see `attr_name=`) and return the graph for method chaining. If `True`, leave node attributes untouched and return the list of visited node IDs in DFS order. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[list[int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=` is `True`: list of node IDs visited in DFS order, starting with `source=`. If `return_list=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~bfs`) : Visit nodes breadth-first, finishing each distance before the next. [](`~dfs_edges`), [](`~dfs_tree`) : The edges of the search tree, as a list or a new graph. [](`~dfs_postorder_nodes`) : The nodes in the order the search finishes them. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a binary tree, DFS dives all the way down the leftmost branch (`1, 2, 4, 8`) before backtracking, which gives a very different order than `bfs()`: ::: {#524bb56e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_balanced_tree(k=2, h=3) graph.dfs(source=1, return_list=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 5, 10, 11, 3, 6, 12, 13, 7, 14, 15] ``` ::: ::: With the default `return_list=False`, the visit order is stored as a node attribute and the graph is returned, so it can be chained straight into a plot. Node 3, the root's second child, is only reached after the whole left subtree: ::: {#e1624b96 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.dfs(source=1).plot( color_by="dfs_order", color_scale="sequential", label_by="label", seed=1, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Watching the search dive Every traversal is recorded in the step log, so `play()` can replay it one visit at a time. Here DFS starts from Central station on the metro map, which stores each station's map position in `pos`. Step through to see the search follow one line as far as it goes before backing up to try another: ::: {#6859d8f7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} metro = ec.metro() metro.note("Follow one line as far as it goes first.").dfs("Central") metro.play(layout="pos") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Directed graphs On a directed graph, DFS only follows edges forward. Starting from `B` reaches `C` and `D` down the chain, while `A` (upstream of `B`) is never visited: ::: {#3c9b1908 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} chain = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")], directed=True ) order = chain.dfs(source="B", return_list=True) [chain.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in order] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['B', 'C', 'D'] ``` ::: :::
